note: Edit the words freely. Keep each line short and kid-friendly. 'rank' decides which theme is shown first when a puzzle has several (lower = first). A theme with 'steps' gets a lesson card; its example position ('ex') is filled in by tools/teach/pick.mjs from real Lichess puzzles.

check.title: Checks
check.hint: A check attacks the king. Look at your pieces one by one. Which of them can reach a square that attacks the king?

check.title: Captures
check.q: Can I capture something, and is it protected?
check.hint: Find enemy pieces you can take. Before you take, ask: can they take me back?

check.title: Threats
check.q: What is my opponent threatening, and what is my best threat?
check.hint: Pretend it is their turn. What would they do to you? Then ask what you can threaten.

check.title: Blunder check
check.hint: After you move, can they capture the piece you moved, or something else you forgot about?

mateIn1.name: Mate in 1
mateIn1.what: You can checkmate the enemy king on your very next move.
mateIn1.spot: Look at every check you can give. Ask: can the king run, block, or capture the checker?
mateIn1.remember: Check every check. One of them is mate!
mateIn1.why: The king is attacked and has nowhere to go, nothing can block, and nothing can capture the checker. That is checkmate, so the game is over.
steps: List every check you can give.
For each check, look at the king's escape squares. Are they all covered or blocked?
Pick the check where nothing can block or capture. That's mate!

mateIn2.name: Mate in 2
mateIn2.what: You can force checkmate in two of your moves, whatever your opponent does.
mateIn2.spot: Start with checks and with moves that take squares away from the king. Then ask: after their reply, do I have mate?
mateIn2.remember: First move squeezes the king. Second move finishes.
mateIn2.why: Your first move leaves the king without a good defence, so whatever your opponent plays, you have a checkmate ready.
steps: Look for checks first, even ones that give up a piece.
After each check, find the king's replies. There are usually only one or two.
Make sure you have mate after every reply. Then play it!

mateIn3.name: Mate in 3
mateIn3.what: You can force checkmate in three of your moves.
mateIn3.spot: Use checks to push the king where you want it. Think about one forcing move at a time.
mateIn3.remember: Keep giving check and the king runs out of room.
mateIn3.why: Each of your moves forces a reply, so the king is steered into a trap and mated on your third move.
steps: Find a check (or a big threat) that forces their reply.
After their reply, look for the next check. The king is being pushed along.
Keep going until the king has no squares left. That's mate!

mateIn4.name: Mate in 4
mateIn4.what: A forced checkmate is hiding four moves deep.
mateIn4.spot: Look for strong checks and sacrifices that rip open the king's cover. Take it one forcing move at a time.
mateIn4.remember: One forcing move at a time.
mateIn4.why: Every move forces a reply, so your opponent can never stop the plan, and it ends in checkmate.

mateIn5.name: Mate in 5 or more
mateIn5.what: A long forced checkmate. It takes five or more moves.
mateIn5.spot: Keep your checks and big threats in mind. If every move forces a reply, you are on the right track.
mateIn5.remember: Stay forcing, and the king cannot escape.
mateIn5.why: Each move forces a reply, so your opponent never gets time to defend, and the king is mated at the end.

backRankMate.name: Back-rank mate
backRankMate.what: Checkmate on the first row, because the king is trapped behind its own pawns.
backRankMate.spot: Look for a king still on its back row with its pawns in front. Can a rook or queen reach that row?
backRankMate.remember: Pawns in front, rook behind: mate on the last row.
backRankMate.why: The king's own pawns block its escape squares, so a rook or queen check along the back row is checkmate.
steps: Find the enemy king. Is it stuck behind its own pawns?
Look for a rook or queen that can reach the back row.
If nothing can block or capture it, give the check. That's mate!

anastasiaMate.name: Anastasia's mate
anastasiaMate.what: A knight and a rook trap the king against the edge of the board.
anastasiaMate.spot: Look for a king on the side of the board next to its own pawn, with a knight and a rook ready to join in.
anastasiaMate.remember: The knight shuts the doors, the rook gives mate.
anastasiaMate.why: The knight covers the squares the king could run to, the king's own piece blocks the other side, and the rook gives check along the edge.
steps: Find a king at the edge of the board with its own piece next to it.
Put a knight where it covers the king's escape squares.
Bring a rook to give check along the edge. That's mate!

arabianMate.name: Arabian mate
arabianMate.what: A knight and a rook checkmate a king in the corner.
arabianMate.spot: Look for a king in the corner. Can a rook check next to it, protected by a knight?
arabianMate.remember: Rook next to the king, knight guards the rook.
arabianMate.why: The rook checks the cornered king, the knight protects the rook so the king cannot take it, and the king has no other square.
steps: Find a king in the corner of the board.
Move your knight to a square that guards the square next to the king.
Put your rook on that square with check. The king can't take it. Mate!

smotheredMate.name: Smothered mate
smotheredMate.what: A knight checkmates a king that is surrounded by its own pieces.
smotheredMate.spot: Look for a king in the corner, boxed in by its own rook and pawns, with a knight that can jump to check.
smotheredMate.remember: The king is smothered by its own friends!
smotheredMate.why: The king's own pieces take away every square, and a knight's check cannot be blocked, so it is checkmate.
steps: Find a king with its own pieces crowded around it.
Look for a knight that can jump to a square giving check.
A knight check cannot be blocked. If the king cannot move, it's mate!

hookMate.name: Hook mate
hookMate.what: A rook, a knight and a pawn work together to checkmate the king.
hookMate.spot: Look for a rook check on the edge that is protected by a knight, with a pawn covering an escape square.
hookMate.remember: Rook gives mate, knight and pawn lock the doors.
hookMate.why: The rook gives check, the knight guards the rook and covers squares, and a pawn takes away another escape square.
steps: Find a king near the edge with few squares to move.
Bring a knight (and a pawn) to cover the squares around the king.
Give check with the rook so the king cannot escape. Mate!

bodenMate.name: Boden's mate
bodenMate.what: Two bishops on crossing diagonals checkmate a king that is boxed in by its own pieces.
bodenMate.spot: Look for a king with its own pieces next to it, and two bishops that can aim at it from different diagonals.
bodenMate.why: One bishop gives check, the other covers the squares the king could use, and the king's own pieces block the rest.
steps: Find a king hemmed in by its own pieces.
Aim one bishop at the king.
Use the other bishop to give check so the crossing diagonals trap the king. Mate!

doubleBishopMate.name: Two-bishop mate
doubleBishopMate.what: Two bishops side by side checkmate the king on the edge of the board.
doubleBishopMate.spot: Look for a king at the edge and two bishops on neighbouring diagonals.
doubleBishopMate.remember: Two bishops, side by side, take away the squares.
doubleBishopMate.why: One bishop checks and the other covers the escape squares, so the king has nowhere to go.
steps: Find a king on the edge of the board.
Put your bishops on neighbouring diagonals.
Give check so the other bishop covers the escape squares. Mate!

dovetailMate.name: Dovetail mate
dovetailMate.what: A queen checks the king from right next to it, while the king's own pieces block the squares on both sides.
dovetailMate.spot: Look for a king with its own pieces beside it. Can your queen reach a square touching the king, with a friend protecting her?
dovetailMate.remember: The queen touches the king, the king's friends are in the way.
dovetailMate.why: The queen is protected so the king cannot take her, and its own pieces block the squares beside it.
steps: Find a king boxed in by its own pieces.
Make sure a piece of yours protects the square next to the king.
Put the queen there with check. The king can't take her. Mate!

operaMate.name: Opera mate
operaMate.what: A bishop and a rook checkmate the king on the edge of the board.
operaMate.spot: Look for a king on the edge, a bishop covering escape squares and a rook that can check.
operaMate.remember: The bishop guards the squares, the rook gives mate.
operaMate.why: The bishop takes away the squares the king could run to, and the rook gives check along the edge.
steps: Find a king on the edge of the board.
Use a bishop to cover the squares next to the king.
Give check with the rook. Mate!

epauletteMate.name: Epaulette mate
epauletteMate.what: The king's own pieces sit on both sides of it like shoulder pads, and a check from the front is mate.
epauletteMate.spot: Look for a king with its own pieces on both sides. Can your queen or rook check it from the front?
epauletteMate.remember: Pieces on both shoulders, check from the front.
epauletteMate.why: The king's own pieces take away both side squares, so a check from the front has no escape.
steps: Find a king with its own pieces on both sides.
Look for a queen or rook that can check from in front.
Make sure the checker is safe. Then play it. Mate!

pillsburysMate.name: Pillsbury's mate
pillsburysMate.what: A rook and a bishop work together to checkmate the king on the edge.
pillsburysMate.spot: Look for a king on the edge with a bishop aimed at it and a rook ready to give check.
pillsburysMate.remember: The bishop stares, the rook strikes.
pillsburysMate.why: The bishop takes away the king's squares and the rook gives the check, so the king cannot escape.

fork.name: Fork
fork.what: One piece attacks two or more enemy pieces at the same time.
fork.spot: Knights are great at forks. Look for a square where one of your pieces can attack two things that are not well protected.
fork.remember: One attacker, two targets. They can only save one!
fork.why: Your forking piece attacks two things at once. Your opponent can only save one of them, so you win the other.
steps: Find two enemy pieces that are valuable or not protected.
Look for one square where a single piece of yours can attack both.
Check that the square is safe, then jump in!

pin.name: Pin
pin.what: A piece cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it on the same line.
pin.spot: Look for bishops, rooks and queens lined up with an enemy piece that has the king or queen behind it.
pin.remember: A pinned piece is stuck in the way.
pin.why: The pinned piece cannot move without losing something bigger, so you can attack it again and again and win it.
steps: Find a long line (diagonal, file or row) with two enemy pieces on it.
If the piece behind is worth more, the one in front is pinned.
Attack the pinned piece again and again until you win it.

skewer.name: Skewer
skewer.what: Like a pin, but the other way round: the valuable piece is in front and must move, so you take the piece behind it.
skewer.spot: Look for a king or queen on the same line as another piece. Attack the big one!
skewer.remember: The big piece runs away, and you take what was behind.
skewer.why: Your attack on the bigger piece forces it to move, and then you capture the piece that was hiding behind it.
steps: Find a king or queen on a line with another piece behind it.
Attack the big piece along that line.
It has to move, so take the piece that was behind it.

discoveredAttack.name: Discovered attack
discoveredAttack.what: You move one piece and uncover an attack from the piece behind it.
discoveredAttack.spot: Look for your bishop, rook or queen hiding behind another of your pieces. The front piece can move with a threat!
discoveredAttack.remember: Move one piece, and two things attack.
discoveredAttack.why: The piece that moved makes its own threat, and the piece behind it now attacks something too. Your opponent cannot answer both.
steps: Find a long-range piece of yours hiding behind another piece of yours.
See what the hidden piece would attack if the front piece moved.
Move the front piece with a threat of its own. Two attacks at once!

discoveredCheck.name: Discovered check
discoveredCheck.what: You move a piece and uncover a check from the piece behind it.
discoveredCheck.spot: Look for your bishop, rook or queen lined up with the enemy king behind one of your own pieces.
discoveredCheck.remember: Open the line and the king is in check!
discoveredCheck.why: The king must answer the check, so the piece that moved is free to do something big, like capturing a queen.
steps: Find your piece lined up with the enemy king, with one of your own pieces in between.
Look at where the front piece could go to make a threat.
Move it! The king must deal with the check, so your threat can't be stopped.

doubleCheck.name: Double check
doubleCheck.what: Two of your pieces give check at the same time.
doubleCheck.spot: Look for a discovered check where the piece that moves also gives check.
doubleCheck.remember: Two checks at once: only the king can move.
doubleCheck.why: You cannot block or capture two checking pieces at once, so the king must move. That often leads to checkmate.
steps: Look for a discovered check.
Check if the piece that moves can also give check.
Play it. Only the king can answer!

deflection.name: Deflection
deflection.what: You force a defender to leave the job it is doing.
deflection.spot: Find an enemy piece guarding something important. Can you attack it or offer it something to take?
deflection.why: The guard has to leave its post, so the piece or square it was protecting is free to take.
steps: Find something important that one enemy piece is guarding.
Think of a way to force that guard to move or to capture something.
When the guard leaves, strike at what it was protecting.

attraction.name: Attraction
attraction.what: You lure an enemy piece, often the king, onto a square where it can be attacked.
attraction.spot: Look for a sacrifice that forces the king or queen to capture and land on a bad square.
attraction.remember: Pull them onto a bad square.
attraction.why: Your move forces their piece to capture and move to a square where you can attack it or checkmate it.
steps: Offer a piece that the king or queen must take.
Look at the square where their piece lands.
Strike at that square with check, a fork or mate.

sacrifice.name: Sacrifice
sacrifice.what: You give up material on purpose to get something bigger back.
sacrifice.spot: Ask: what do I get if they take? Look for check, mate, or winning more than you gave.
sacrifice.remember: Give a little, win a lot.
sacrifice.why: The piece you give up pulls the enemy out of position or opens a path, and you win more than you lost.
steps: Pick the piece you could give up. Which squares or lines does it open?
Count what happens if your opponent takes it. Do you get check or a bigger win?
Only sacrifice if you can see the payoff. Never guess!

hangingPiece.name: Hanging piece
hangingPiece.what: A piece that is not protected, so you can take it for free.
hangingPiece.spot: Before every move ask: which of their pieces has no protector? Which of mine?
hangingPiece.why: The piece had no defender, so taking it costs you nothing.
steps: Look at every enemy piece. Is it protected by anything?
Find an unprotected piece you can attack or take.
Before you take, check that you are not leaving something of yours hanging.

trappedPiece.name: Trapped piece
trappedPiece.what: A piece that is attacked and has no safe square to run to.
trappedPiece.spot: Look for enemy pieces near the edge or surrounded by pawns. Attack them.
trappedPiece.why: Every square the piece could run to is covered, so you win it.
steps: Find an enemy piece with very few squares to move to.
Count its escape squares. Are they all covered?
Attack it. It cannot get away!

clearance.name: Clearance
clearance.what: You move a piece out of the way so another piece can use a square or a line.
clearance.spot: Ask: is one of my own pieces blocking a good move for another piece?
clearance.remember: Clear the road, then drive through.
clearance.why: Moving the blocker with a threat, often a check, lets your other piece reach its square without losing time.
steps: Find a great square or line that one of your pieces cannot reach.
See which of your own pieces is in the way.
Move it with a threat so your opponent has no time to react.

capturingDefender.name: Remove the defender
capturingDefender.what: You take away a piece that is protecting something.
capturingDefender.spot: Find a piece you want to win. Who is protecting it? Can you take that protector?
capturingDefender.remember: Take the guard, then take the prize.
capturingDefender.why: Once the defender is gone, the piece it was protecting can be captured.
steps: Pick the piece you want to win.
Find the piece that protects it.
Take or chase the protector, then win the prize.

intermezzo.name: In-between move
intermezzo.what: Instead of the expected move, you play a stronger move first.
intermezzo.spot: Before you take back, ask: is there a check or a threat I can make first?
intermezzo.why: The extra move, often a check, wins something, and you can still make the move you planned afterwards.
steps: Notice the move everyone expects, like taking back a piece.
Look for a check or a threat you could play first.
Play it. Your opponent must answer, and you win something extra.

xRayAttack.name: X-ray
xRayAttack.what: A piece attacks through another piece, as if it had x-ray eyes.
xRayAttack.spot: Look along a line past the first piece. What is behind it?
xRayAttack.remember: Look through the first piece. What is behind it?
xRayAttack.why: Your piece keeps up pressure on a square or piece behind another piece, so trades on that square work out in your favour.
steps: Pick a line where one of your long-range pieces looks past an enemy piece.
See what is hiding behind it.
Use that hidden pressure when pieces are traded.

interference.name: Interference
interference.what: You put a piece between two enemy pieces so they can no longer protect each other.
interference.spot: Find two enemy pieces that protect each other along a line. Can you step in between?
interference.why: The piece you place in between cuts the connection, so one enemy piece loses its protection.
steps: Find two enemy pieces that guard each other along a line.
Look for a safe square on that line between them.
Put a piece there, then win the piece that lost its protection.

quietMove.name: Quiet move
quietMove.what: A calm move, not a check or a capture, that sets up a strong threat.
quietMove.spot: When there are no good checks or captures, look for a move that creates a threat your opponent cannot stop.
quietMove.why: It does not look scary, but it prepares a threat your opponent cannot stop.
steps: Look for checks and captures first. If none work, don't panic.
Ask: what threat could I make that they cannot stop?
Play the quiet move and let the threat do the work.

defensiveMove.name: Defensive move
defensiveMove.what: The best move is to defend, not to attack.
defensiveMove.spot: Ask what your opponent is threatening first. Can you stop it?
defensiveMove.remember: Stop their plan before you start yours.
defensiveMove.why: The move stops your opponent's threat and keeps your advantage.
steps: Ask: what is my opponent threatening?
Find a move that stops it. Check whether it is safe.
Only then think about your own attack.

zugzwang.name: Zugzwang
zugzwang.what: Every move your opponent can make makes their position worse.
zugzwang.spot: Look for positions where it would be great if it were your opponent's turn to move and they had to give something up.
zugzwang.remember: Sometimes you must move, and that hurts.
zugzwang.why: Your opponent has to move, and every move loses something. Waiting with a useful move made it work.
steps: Count the safe moves your opponent has. Are there very few?
Find a move that keeps everything safe and passes the turn to them.
Now they must make a move that hurts.

exposedKing.name: Exposed king
exposedKing.what: The enemy king has lost its pawn cover and is easy to attack.
exposedKing.spot: Look for kings with missing pawns in front of them. Which of your pieces can join the attack?
exposedKing.remember: A king without cover is in danger.
exposedKing.why: Few pieces guard the king, so checks and threats quickly become dangerous.
steps: Look at the pawns in front of the enemy king. Are some missing?
Bring your pieces closer, or look for checks.
Keep making threats so the king never gets to hide.

attackingF2F7.name: Attack on f2/f7
attackingF2F7.what: At the start of the game, only the king guards the f2 and f7 squares, so they are weak.
attackingF2F7.spot: Look for a bishop, knight or queen that can hit f2 (against White) or f7 (against Black).
attackingF2F7.remember: f2 and f7 are weak spots at the start.
attackingF2F7.why: Only the king guards that square, so an attack there is hard to stop.
steps: Look at f7 (or f2). Who guards it?
Aim your pieces at it, such as a bishop and a queen.
If only the king guards it, you can win material or even checkmate.

kingsideAttack.name: Kingside attack
kingsideAttack.what: An attack on the enemy king after it has castled on the right-hand side of the board.
kingsideAttack.spot: Look for ways to bring many of your pieces near the enemy king.
kingsideAttack.remember: Bring many pieces to the attack.
kingsideAttack.why: Several of your pieces aim at the king's corner, so the defence breaks.
steps: Count your pieces that can reach the enemy king.
Bring more pieces closer.
Look for checks and sacrifices that crack open the king's cover.

queensideAttack.name: Queenside attack
queensideAttack.what: An attack on the enemy king after it has castled on the left-hand side of the board.
queensideAttack.spot: Look for ways to bring your pieces near the enemy king.
queensideAttack.remember: Bring many pieces to the attack.
queensideAttack.why: Several of your pieces aim at the king's corner, so the defence breaks.

advancedPawn.name: Advanced pawn
advancedPawn.what: A pawn deep in enemy land that is close to turning into a queen.
advancedPawn.spot: Look for pawns near the last row. Can they be helped, or do they distract the enemy?
advancedPawn.remember: A pawn near the end is a big danger.
advancedPawn.why: The pawn is so close to promoting that the opponent must deal with it, and that gives you time or wins material.
steps: Find a pawn that is close to the last row.
See which squares in front of it are free or guarded.
Help it forward, or use the threat to win something.

promotion.name: Promotion
promotion.what: A pawn reaches the last row and turns into a new piece.
promotion.spot: Look for pawns that are a step or two from the last row.
promotion.remember: A pawn at the end becomes a queen!
promotion.why: Reaching the last row makes a new queen (or another piece) and changes the game.

rookEndgame.name: Rook endgame
rookEndgame.what: An ending where each side has a rook and some pawns.
rookEndgame.spot: Keep your rook active and your king close to the pawns.
rookEndgame.why: In rook endgames, exact moves and an active rook decide the game.

pawnEndgame.name: Pawn endgame
pawnEndgame.what: An ending with only kings and pawns.
pawnEndgame.spot: Kings are strong here. Count moves carefully and use your king.
pawnEndgame.remember: In pawn endings, the king is a fighter.
pawnEndgame.why: With only pawns left, one extra step by the king or a pawn can decide the game, so counting matters.

queenEndgame.name: Queen endgame
queenEndgame.what: An ending where each side has a queen and some pawns.
queenEndgame.spot: Look for checks, and keep your king safe from them.
queenEndgame.remember: With queens on, checks are everywhere.
queenEndgame.why: Queens can check from far away, so the best move often uses checks to win pawns or force a draw.

bishopEndgame.name: Bishop endgame
bishopEndgame.what: An ending with bishops and pawns.
bishopEndgame.spot: Notice which colour your bishop moves on, and where the pawns are.
bishopEndgame.remember: A bishop stays on one colour.
bishopEndgame.why: Bishops only travel on one colour, so which squares they control decides the ending.

knightEndgame.name: Knight endgame
knightEndgame.what: An ending with knights and pawns.
knightEndgame.spot: Knights are slow. Count how many jumps you need.
knightEndgame.remember: Knights are slow, so count the jumps.
knightEndgame.why: Knights need several moves to cross the board, so counting jumps decides who gets there first.

queenRookEndgame.name: Queen and rook endgame
queenRookEndgame.what: An ending where each side has a queen and a rook.
queenRookEndgame.spot: Look for checks and keep your king covered.
queenRookEndgame.why: With a queen and a rook, a single check can win a piece or start a mating attack.

enPassant.name: En passant
enPassant.what: A special pawn capture: a pawn that just moved two squares can be taken as if it had moved only one.
enPassant.spot: It can only be done on the very next move.
enPassant.remember: Now or never: en passant must happen right away.
enPassant.why: The special capture is the only way to take that pawn, and it only works on the move right after the pawn jumps.

castling.name: Castling
castling.what: The king and a rook move together in one move.
castling.spot: It puts your king in a safer place and brings the rook into play.
castling.remember: Castle early to keep the king safe.
castling.why: Castling moves the king to safety and the rook to the middle in a single move.
